gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 in the recommended kit charges only from 0°C to 40°C (32–104°F) and takes solar only at 12–28 V and 10 A. So the station has to sit in shade while the panel sits in the sun, and a second panel must be wired in parallel, not in series.
standout_why: I compared against the cited rivals solar-home.space, campequipmentplus.com and solutionenergy.com, and against our own current page. None gives a charging temperature window for any small LiFePO4 station. solutionenergy has only a fast-charge note for Anker (battery above 68°F). None gives a solar input voltage window or open-circuit voltage (Voc) limit for any pick: campequipmentplus says only that 'Input voltage range' matters, with no figures, and solar-home says 'keep the panel within the solar input your unit lists'. None gives self-consumption figures. Our current page says 'CPAP one night' and '~4 hours of full sun' without any of these limits.
decides: This keeps the Elite 30 V2 + 100 W kit as the pick. Its 100 W panel sits within the 12–28 V, 10 A, 200 W input. The finding adds two conditions for whether the plan works at a tent site. (1) Charging stops when the station is above 104°F or below 32°F, so the station goes in shade on a long cable while the panel is in the sun, and frosty mornings give no charge until the battery warms. (2) An upgrade to 200 W of panels means two panels in parallel, never in series, because two ~20 V panels in series exceed the 28 V open-circuit limit. The manual's own runtime figure of about 9 W self-consumption also takes roughly 90 Wh out of 288 Wh over a 10-hour night on the inverter. That trims the 'CPAP one night' claim: a CPAP should run from the 12 V port where possible.

findings.label: Solar input window (maker's US site)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI blog: connecting solar panels to solar generator (Bluetti Team, dated 2026-11-04)
findings.note: Table row quoted: 'Elite 30 V2 | 200 W | 10 A | 12 V - 28 V'. The same article says series wiring raises voltage and parallel raises current, and that total voltage must stay within the unit's range. Two 100 W panels with roughly 20+ V open-circuit each would total over 28 V in series, so they must go in parallel. The ~20 V per-panel figure is typical for 100 W panels; I didn't source it for the kit's panel.
